summary: This informational document offers guidance on developing privacy considerations for protocol specifications. It aims to make designers, implementers, and users of Internet protocols aware of privacy-related design choices. It suggests whether a given RFC needs a privacy considerations section depends on its content.

plainLanguage.summary: Security protects a system; privacy protects the people who use it. This memo is the reference on the second subject. It lists the ways a network protocol can harm users, such as watching them, linking their separate activities together, or revealing more than they meant to, and then gives advice on designing protocols to avoid that harm. Many working groups use it when reviewing a new protocol for privacy.

subtitle: How to think about privacy when designing Internet protocols: the threats to watch for and the guidelines that reduce them.

tldr.problem: Protocol designers usually think in terms of security threats to systems, but the data their protocols expose can also harm the people who use them, and the two areas are related but not the same.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lays out a communications model, a catalogue of eleven privacy threats, mitigations such as data minimization, anonymity and pseudonymity, and a set of guidelines for protocol designers.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC from July 2013 that is widely used as the reference text for privacy reviews of new Internet protocols.

today: RFC 6973 is an Informational RFC published in July 2013, and the unit metadata records no successor or update. It is widely referenced by later protocol specifications in their own privacy considerations sections, which apply the vocabulary and threat list defined here.

sections.title: Privacy as a Design Concern
sections.content:
This document provides privacy considerations for the designers and implementers of Internet protocols. It complements the practice of writing security considerations, but it is distinct: a protocol can be perfectly secure against attackers and still harm the privacy of the people who use it, because the issue is what information the protocol reveals and to whom.

The memo is written for a technical audience and it approaches the subject through a model of communication and a catalogue of threats. It does not prescribe a single right answer, because privacy expectations differ between applications and communities. Instead it gives a vocabulary and a list of questions that designers can use to reason about the effects of their choices.

The document is Informative, and it is intended to be applied alongside the security considerations that every protocol specification already carries. Its concepts include vocabulary for the entities involved in the communication, the data that flows between them and the analysis that can be performed on that data.
sections.plainLanguage: A protocol can be technically safe and still expose its users. This memo exists to make that second kind of harm visible, by giving protocol designers a shared set of ideas and questions to work through while a protocol is still being designed.

sections.title: The Communications Model
sections.content:
The memo begins by setting out the parties and the data. Entities include the initiator and responder in a communication, and also the intermediaries, such as relays and proxies, that may observe or handle the traffic. The data and analysis part draws a distinction between the data that is carried and the conclusions that can be drawn from it, since the same data can support very different inferences in different contexts.

Central to the discussion is identifiability. Information that identifies a person is troubling because it links activity to a who. But information does not have to carry a name to matter: anything that is stable enough to be recognized again, such as a persistent identifier or an unusual pattern of behaviour, can single a person out or group their activities together. The memo therefore treats identifiers and linkability as the heart of the problem, and it notes that even data that looks anonymous can become identifying when combined with other data.

From this model the memo builds a communications model that maps who talks to whom, through what middle parties, and what each of them can observe. A designer who can draw that picture can start asking where personal data appears and what happens to it along the path.
sections.plainLanguage: The mental picture is a conversation with several parties on the path, not just the two ends. The key idea is that something does not have to be a name to identify a person; any value or habit that stays the same from one time to the next can be used to recognize them, and pieces that look harmless alone can combine to reveal a lot.

sections.title: The Privacy Threats
sections.content:
The memo sets out two groups of threats. The first are shared with security: surveillance, meaning the ongoing collection of data about a person's activities; stored data compromise, where data an operator has collected is exposed by an attack; intrusion, where an attacker gains access to private data on a device; and misattribution, where the record of an action is attributed wrongly, for example because a shared address is attributed to a single person.

The second group is specific to privacy and does not map onto a security property in the same way. Correlation combines separate pieces of information about a person, sometimes from different contexts, to build a larger picture. Identification links data to a specific individual. Secondary use is the use of data for a purpose other than the one it was collected for. Disclosure is the revealing of information to a party the person did not intend to reach, including through settings that are easy to get wrong. Exclusion is the failure to give a person the chance to participate in decisions about their own data, for instance because a service cannot be used without agreeing to disclose something.

These threats are presented as a checklist to run through when thinking about a protocol, not as a claim that every protocol suffers all of them. The severity of each depends on the context in which the protocol is used.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two families of danger. One is shared with ordinary security: being watched, having stored data stolen, being broken into, or being wrongly blamed. The other is specific to privacy: joining separate clues about a person together, picking a person out, using data for a purpose it was not collected for, letting it reach more people than intended, and leaving the person no say.

sections.title: Mitigations
sections.content:
The main mitigation the memo offers is data minimization: collect and reveal as little personal data as the purpose requires. Under that heading it describes anonymity, where a person cannot be singled out within a set of others and so cannot be recognized across interactions; pseudonymity, where a persistent but unlinked name is used so that actions can be grouped without revealing the real identity; and identity confidentiality, which keeps the identities of the parties hidden from observers. Identity management systems get their own discussion because they are a common place where more data than necessary is collected and kept.

The memo also treats user participation and security as mitigations. User participation means giving people a say in what is done with their data, including the ability to understand and control it. Security appears here because it cuts both ways: the mechanisms that protect data, such as proving who someone is, can themselves create linkable identifiers, so a designer has to look at the privacy effect of a security measure, not only its protective value.

Both anonymity and pseudonymity have limits. A pseudonym is not anonymity, because a pseudonym links a person's own actions to each other, and it can be unmasked if the link to the real identity is recorded or inferred.
sections.plainLanguage: The main defence is to collect and reveal as little as possible. A designer can make a user hard to pick out among many, give them a nickname that is not tied to their real identity, or keep identities hidden from observers. Security measures help, but they can also create values that make a person easier to follow, so their privacy cost has to be weighed.

sections.title: Guidelines for Designers
sections.content:
The memo closes with guidelines divided into data minimization, user participation, security and general advice. The data-minimization guidance asks designers to question whether an item of data is needed at all, to avoid identifiers that persist longer or are visible more widely than necessary, to prefer values that change or are shared among many users, to provide anonymity or pseudonymity where appropriate, and to consider how data will be combined with information from other sources. The user-participation guidance asks designers to give users meaningful choices and to make sure a refusal does not shut them out of unrelated functions.

The security guidance reminds designers that mechanisms such as authentication and anti-abuse measures can create linkable data, and it argues for keeping security without unnecessary exposure. The general guidance asks designers to document the privacy considerations of a protocol and to revisit them as the protocol evolves. The memo includes a worked example to show how the threats and mitigations can be applied to a concrete case.

Throughout, the memo is careful to say that privacy is context dependent. The same header, log entry or identifier can be harmless in one application and revealing in another, so the guidelines are meant to prompt thought rather than to supply mechanical rules. The section closes the document's substantive advice; the RFC states that it raises the privacy issues it describes rather than presenting a protocol of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice comes down to a few habits: ask whether each piece of data is truly needed, prefer values that are shared or change over time, give users real choices, watch for security features that quietly make users easier to track, and write down the privacy reasoning. The same detail can be harmless in one setting and revealing in another, so the point is to think it through, not to follow a fixed rulebook.
